Case Vignette: Ms. A.

Ms. A. is a 67-year-old married South Asian woman who works as a program coordinator for a small non-profit organization focused on refugee resettlement. She has been attending weekly therapy sessions for the past month, referred by her primary care physician after reporting persistent insomnia and "a feeling of being on edge all the time." She is a small, neat woman who speaks softly, often folding her hands in her lap as she talks.

The traumatic event occurred two years ago, but Ms. A. has only recently begun to speak about it. She was walking home from the non-profit office late one evening after a community dinner event. A man she did not know approached her from behind as she unlocked her apartment building door. He forced her inside the vestibule, pressed a hand over her mouth, and sexually assaulted her. She remembers the cold concrete floor against her back, the smell of cigarette smoke on his jacket, and the sound of a distant siren that never seemed to get closer. She did not scream. She did not fight. She "just went numb," she says, and waited for it to be over.

In the weeks after the assault, Ms. A. did not tell anyone. Not her husband, not her adult children, not her colleagues. She felt a deep, suffocating shame—a sense that she had somehow invited the attack by being out so late, by being a woman alone. She cleaned her own clothes, scrubbed her own skin raw in the shower, and returned to work the next day as if nothing had happened. She told herself the memory would fade, that she could simply "move on."

It has not faded. In the present, Ms. A. describes a constant state of hypervigilance. She cannot walk to her car in the parking lot without checking the back seat three times. She no longer attends evening events for her non-profit, citing vague "health concerns" to her supervisor. Her husband, a kind but distracted man, has noticed she flinches when he touches her shoulder unexpectedly, but she brushes it off as "bad nerves." She has stopped wearing the perfume she wore that night—a jasmine scent her daughter gave her—because the smell instantly transports her back to the vestibule.

Her work, once a source of purpose, has become a minefield. One of her clients, a young woman from Syria, was recently placed in a new apartment. When Ms. A. visited the building, she found the hallway smelled faintly of cigarette smoke. She froze at the door, unable to enter, her heart pounding so hard she thought she might vomit. She told the client she was feeling unwell and left. She now avoids that building entirely, assigning a colleague to handle the case without explanation.

At home, her sleep is fractured. She wakes at 3:00 a.m. most nights, drenched in sweat, with the sensation of a hand over her mouth. She has learned to lie perfectly still so as not to wake her husband. She does not tell him about the nightmares. She tells no one. She has begun to wonder if she is "going crazy," a fear that feels more immediate than the memory of the assault itself.

During our sessions, Ms. A. speaks in a flat, measured tone, as if reciting someone else's story. She avoids eye contact when describing the assault. She often pauses, then says, "I should be over this by now. It was two years. Other people have real problems." She cannot cry in session. She says she hasn't cried since the night it happened. She is not depressed, she insists—just "tired." But her PCL-5 score of 70 reflects severe symptom burden across all four clusters: intrusion, avoidance, negative alterations in cognition and mood, and marked alterations in arousal and reactivity.

She is a woman who has spent a lifetime holding things together—her family, her community, her work. Now, she is holding a secret that is slowly pulling her apart, piece by piece, in the quiet hours of the night.
